idiom_name: AtomicReference.getAndSet or @Volatile var with a single producer
implementation_notes: Kotlin maps onto the JVM primitives directly: publish an immutable snapshot with `AtomicReference.getAndSet`/`updateAndGet`, or - with exactly one producer - declare `@Volatile` (Kotlin's alias for the JVM field modifier) and assign the finished frame, giving readers cheap volatile reads. For coroutines the official guidance is the same discipline: shared mutable state must be confined or protected, and `Mutex.withLock` (suspending, non-reentrant) is the tool when several fields must move as one unit; `volatile` only guarantees visibility of the reference, not atomicity of larger actions, as the concurrency guide states explicitly. Garbage collection removes buffer-lifetime bookkeeping; only the 'never mutate a published frame' convention remains.
pitfalls: `@Volatile` is visibility, not atomicity: a multi-field or read-modify-write update still needs a lock or an atomic type.
`kotlinx.coroutines.Mutex` is suspending and not reentrant; holding it across a suspension that re-enters it deadlocks.
A delegated property whose setter does extra work turns one assignment into several operations - an apparently atomic write stops being one.

variants.name: Android SurfaceHolder lockCanvas/unlockCanvasAndPost
variants.implementation_notes: On Android the platform owns the buffers: `SurfaceHolder.lockCanvas()` returns the canvas of the surface's back buffer, and `unlockCanvasAndPost(canvas)` 'finish[es] editing pixels in the surface' and posts the frame to the compositor. The contract is the lock/unlock window - draw the whole frame between the two calls, never touch the canvas afterwards, and use `try`/`finally`; rendering runs off the UI thread while the `SurfaceView` owns the layout. The same shape appears in `TextureView`, and in Compose the framework handles buffering entirely.
pitfalls: A missed `unlockCanvasAndPost` (exception path) leaves the surface unpostable - always pair them in `finally`.
`lockCanvas` returns null when the surface is not ready; drawing on a retained canvas after the surface is destroyed crashes or corrupts the buffer.
Calling `lockCanvas` from several threads, or drawing after unlock, races with the compositor; keep one producer per surface.
Software canvas locking is slower than GPU paths (SurfaceTexture, Compose, OpenGL) - use it for simple 2D layers, not for high frame rates.
